textPlacement.assessment: Pass. “Getting dressed together” immediately names the parent subject. Both topic rows replace repeated generic participation language with a reach toward a shirt or an arm into a sleeve, retain invitation and help as needed, and do not imply a required milestone at 6–9 months. The brief cue is an ordinary dressing situation. The full entry keeps suitable choices, gentle hands, time for a response, proportionate help and the necessary-care limit. The displayed age context distinguishes the infant-wide passage from the nine-month sleeve example. The invitation remains natural and usable without adding a dressing procedure.

resolutions.surface: 6–9 months / Everyday care and Connection & feelings topic rows and detail header/context
resolutions.assessment: The exact replacement title names dressing, the summary names reaching toward a shirt or an arm into a sleeve, and the cue simply names changing clothes. The repeated “small part” and “room for” wording is removed from these fields; help, invitation and necessary care remain visible. Reviewed in both actual topic rows and the full entry.

textPlacement.assessment: Pass. “Beginning solid foods” identifies the subject without telling the parent to start. Both Everyday care and Play & discovery rows independently retain author attribution, waiting until six months and signs of readiness, manageable food, the baby’s pace, and the book’s adjoining choking precautions and learning-first-aid context. The row no longer depends on the detail for that sensitive qualification. The full entry still distinguishes early food interest from readiness, keeps help suited to coordination and describes sensory/language/hand-use meaning without supplying a feeding or emergency procedure. The age context makes clear that reaching or age alone does not settle readiness.

textPlacement.assessment: Pass. The visible title and both rows describe a recognizable meal situation; throwing remains a possible sign of completion, with uncertainty stated in the short surface itself. Removing the unexplained eating-time-example sentence makes the detail read naturally. The remaining text retains the authors’ adult/baby division of responsibility, opposition to pressing or distracting a baby into eating, and a tentative, responsive ending to the meal. No clock target or certain behavioral explanation has been introduced. The 6–9-month placement uses situational observation; the separate 9-to-12-month language reference does not become a milestone claim.

textPlacement.assessment: Pass. “Your baby’s daily rhythm” makes the subject identifiable at a glance. Both topic rows retain a changing feeding/play/sleep rhythm, familiar transition cues and the explicit distinction from a timetable. The detail allows variation, travel and home changes, coordinates with caregivers only where possible, and treats family rituals as inclusive examples. The displayed age context remains infant-wide and responsive to this baby and the family’s circumstances. The title change does not turn the source’s flexible description into a scheduled routine.

limitations: This is a bounded tone/spirit review of four exact text components, not publication approval or independent medical verification. Art is absent, so there is no art verdict. Retained read logs explicitly link this same reviewer’s earlier complete original-page reads and do not claim new reading; fresh logs record only pages actually reread for this renewal. Source-only sensitive meaning is judged on each short surface as well as the detail. No other batch or reviewer finding is resolved.
